title: V. The Third Ordeal
paragraphs: Though Mitya spoke sullenly, it was clear he was trying harder than ever not to forget or leave out a single detail of his story. He told them how he'd leapt over the fence into his father's garden, how he'd approached the window, told them everything that had happened beneath it. Clearly, precisely, distinctly, he described the feelings that had tormented him during those minutes in the garden, when he'd longed so desperately to know whether Grushenka was with his father or not. But, strangely enough, both lawyers now listened with a kind of grim reserve, looking at him coldly, asking few questions. Mitya couldn't read anything from their faces.
"They're angry and offended," he thought. "Well, to hell with them!"

When he described how he'd finally decided to give his father the "signal" that Grushenka had arrived, so he'd open the window, the lawyers paid no attention at all to the word "signal," as though they'd entirely missed its meaning in this context — so much so that Mitya noticed it. Coming at last to the moment when, seeing his father peering out the window, his hatred had flared up and he'd pulled the pestle from his pocket, he suddenly, almost deliberately, stopped short. He sat staring at the wall, aware that their eyes were fixed on him.
"Well?" said the investigating lawyer. "You pulled out the weapon and ... and then what happened?"
"Then? Why, then I murdered him ... struck him on the head and cracked his skull.... I suppose that's the story you've got. That's it!"
His eyes suddenly flashed. All his suppressed rage suddenly blazed up in his soul with extraordinary violence.
"Our story?" repeated Nikolay Parfenovitch. "Well — and yours?"
Mitya dropped his eyes and stayed silent a long while.

"My story, gentlemen? Well, it was like this," he began softly. "Whether it was someone's tears, or my mother praying to God, or a good angel kissing me at that instant, I don't know. But the devil was defeated. I rushed away from the window and ran for the fence. My father was startled, and for the first time saw me right then, cried out, and jumped back from the window. I remember that very clearly. I ran across the garden to the fence ... and that's where Grigory caught me, while I was sitting on the fence."
At that point he finally raised his eyes and looked at his listeners. They seemed to be watching him with perfectly unruffled attention. A kind of fit of indignation seized Mitya's soul.
"Why, you're laughing at me right now, gentlemen!" he broke off suddenly.
"What makes you say that?" Nikolay Parfenovitch observed.

"You don't believe a single word — that's why! I understand, of course, that I've reached the crucial point. The old man's lying there now with his skull broken, while I — after dramatically describing how I wanted to kill him and how I snatched up the pestle — suddenly run away from the window. A romance! Poetry! As if anyone could just take a fellow's word for it. Ha ha! You're mockers, gentlemen!"
And he swung round in his chair so hard it creaked.
"And did you notice," the prosecutor asked suddenly, as though not registering Mitya's agitation, "did you notice, when you ran from the window, whether the door into the garden was open?"
"No, it wasn't open."
"It wasn't?"
"It was shut. And who could have opened it? Bah! The door. Wait a moment!" he seemed suddenly struck by a thought, and almost with a start:
"Wait — did you find the door open?"
"Yes, it was open."
"Then who could have opened it, if not one of you?" cried Mitya, greatly astonished.

"The door stood open, and your father's killer undoubtedly went in through that door, and, having committed the crime, went out again the same way," the prosecutor pronounced deliberately, as though chiseling out each word one by one. "That's perfectly clear. The murder was committed inside the room, not through the window — that's beyond doubt from the examination that's been carried out, from the position of the body, from everything. There's no question about that fact."
Mitya was utterly dumbfounded.

"But that's absolutely impossible!" he cried, completely at a loss. "I ... I didn't go in.... I'm telling you positively, definitely, the door was shut the whole time I was in the garden, and when I ran out of the garden too. I only stood at the window and saw him through it. That's all, that's all.... I remember it down to the last minute. And even if I didn't remember, it would still be true. I know it, because no one knew the signals except Smerdyakov, me, and the dead man. And he wouldn't have opened that door to anyone on earth without the signal."

"Signals? What signals?" the prosecutor asked, with a greedy, almost hysterical, curiosity. He instantly dropped every trace of his reserve and dignity. He asked the question with a kind of cringing timidity. He sensed an important fact he'd known nothing about, and was already dreading that Mitya might refuse to disclose it.

"So you didn't know!" Mitya winked at him, with a malicious, mocking smile. "And what if I don't tell you? Who could you possibly find out from? No one knew about the signals except my father, Smerdyakov, and me — that's all. Heaven knew too, but Heaven won't tell you. Still, it's an interesting fact. No telling what you might build on it. Ha ha! Take heart, gentlemen, I'll reveal it. You've got some foolish notion in your hearts. You don't know the man you're dealing with! You're dealing with a prisoner who gives evidence against himself, to his own detriment! Yes, because I'm a man of honor, and you — are not."

The prosecutor swallowed this without a word. He was trembling with impatience to hear the new fact. Minutely, at length, Mitya told them everything about the signals Fyodor Pavlovitch had devised for Smerdyakov. He told them exactly what each tap on the window meant, tapped the signals out on the table, and when Nikolay Parfenovitch asked whether he supposed he, Mitya, had tapped the signal for "Grushenka has come" when he knocked at his father's window, he answered flatly that yes, he had tapped that very signal, "Grushenka has come."
"So now you can build your tower," Mitya broke off, and again turned away from them with contempt.
"So no one knew of the signals besides your late father, you, and the valet Smerdyakov? No one else?" Nikolay Parfenovitch asked once more.
"Yes. The valet Smerdyakov, and Heaven. Write down about Heaven. That might come in useful. Besides, you'll need God yourselves, before this is over."
And they had, of course, already begun writing it down. But as they wrote, the prosecutor suddenly said, as though hitting on a new idea:

"But if Smerdyakov also knew about these signals, and you flatly deny any responsibility for your father's death, isn't it possible he was the one who tapped the agreed signal, got your father to open the door to him, and then ... committed the crime?"
Mitya turned on him a look of deep irony and intense hatred. His silent stare went on so long it made the prosecutor blink.

"You've caught the fox again," Mitya finally remarked; "you've got the beast by the tail. Ha ha! I see right through you, Mr. Prosecutor. You thought, of course, that I'd jump at that, snatch up your prompt, and shout at the top of my lungs, 'Aie, it's Smerdyakov! He's the murderer!' Admit that's what you thought. Admit it, and I'll go on."
But the prosecutor didn't admit it. He held his tongue and waited.
"You're mistaken. I'm not going to shout 'It's Smerdyakov,'" said Mitya.
"And you don't even suspect him?"
"Why, do you suspect him?"
"He's under suspicion too."
Mitya fixed his eyes on the floor.

"Joking aside," he brought out, gloomily. "Listen. From the very start, almost from the moment I ran out to you from behind the curtain, the thought of Smerdyakov has been in my mind. I've been sitting here shouting that I'm innocent, and thinking, the whole time, 'Smerdyakov!' I can't get him out of my head. In fact, I thought of Smerdyakov just now too; but only for a second. Almost right away I thought, 'No, it's not Smerdyakov.' It's not his doing, gentlemen."
"In that case, is there anyone else you suspect?" Nikolay Parfenovitch asked, cautiously.
"I don't know who it could be — whether it's the hand of Heaven or of Satan, but ... not Smerdyakov," Mitya bit off, with decision.
"But what makes you say so, so confidently, so emphatically, that it's not him?"

"From my own conviction — my own impression. Because Smerdyakov is a man of the most abject character, and a coward. He's not just a coward, he's the sum total of all the cowardice in the world walking around on two legs. He has the heart of a chicken. Whenever he talked to me, he was always trembling, afraid I'd kill him, though I never once raised a hand against him. He fell at my feet and blubbered; he's literally kissed these very boots, begging me 'not to frighten him.' Do you hear that? 'Not to frighten him.' What a thing to say! Why, I even offered him money. He's a sniveling chicken — sickly, epileptic, feeble-minded — an eight-year-old child could thrash him. He hasn't got a character worth mentioning. It's not Smerdyakov, gentlemen. He doesn't care for money; he wouldn't even take gifts from me. Besides, what motive would he have to murder the old man? Why, he's very likely his son, you know — his natural son. Did you know that?"
"We've heard that story. But you're your father's son too, you know — and yet you yourself told everyone you meant to murder him."

"That's a low blow! And a nasty, mean one too! But I'm not afraid! Oh, gentlemen, isn't it rather base of you to say that to my face? It's base, because I told you that myself. I not only wanted to murder him, I might have done it. And what's more, I went out of my way to tell you, unprompted, that I very nearly murdered him. But, you see, I didn't murder him; you see, my guardian angel saved me — that's what you haven't taken into account. And that's exactly why it's base of you to say it. Because I didn't kill him, I didn't kill him! Do you hear me — I did not kill him."
He was nearly choking. He hadn't been so moved at any point during the whole interrogation.
"And what has he told you, gentlemen — Smerdyakov, I mean?" he added suddenly, after a pause. "May I ask that?"

"You may ask any question," the prosecutor replied, with cold severity, "any question relating to the facts of the case, and we are, I repeat, obligated to answer every inquiry you make. We found the servant Smerdyakov, whom you're asking about, lying unconscious in his bed, in an epileptic fit of extreme severity, which had apparently recurred perhaps ten times over. The doctor who was with us told us, after examining him, that he may not survive the night."
"Well, if that's so, the devil himself must have killed him," burst suddenly from Mitya, as if until that very moment he'd still been asking himself: "Was it Smerdyakov, or not?"
"We'll come back to this later," Nikolay Parfenovitch decided. "Now, would you care to continue your statement?"

Mitya asked for a rest. His request was politely granted. After resting, he went on with his story. But he was plainly depressed. He was exhausted, humiliated, morally shaken. To make matters worse, the prosecutor seemed to be deliberately needling him with irritating interruptions over "trivial points." Mitya had barely finished describing how, sitting astride the wall, he'd struck Grigory on the head with the pestle while the old man gripped his left leg, and how he'd then jumped down to look at him, when the prosecutor stopped him to ask him to describe exactly how he'd been sitting on the wall. Mitya was taken aback.
"Oh, I was sitting like this, straddling it, one leg on each side of the wall."
"And the pestle?"
"The pestle was in my hand."
"Not in your pocket? Do you remember that precisely? Was it a hard blow you gave him?"
"It must have been a hard one. But why do you ask?"
"Would you mind sitting on the chair the way you sat on the wall then, and showing us exactly how you moved your arm, and in which direction?"
"You're making fun of me, aren't you?" Mitya asked, looking haughtily at the man; but the other didn't flinch.
Mitya turned abruptly, straddled the chair, and swung his arm.
"This is how I struck him! This is how I knocked him down! What more do you want?"
"Thank you. May I trouble you now to explain why you jumped down, for what purpose, and what you intended?"
"Oh, hang it!... I jumped down to look at the man I'd hurt ... I don't know what for!"
"Even though you were so agitated and were running away?"
"Yes, even though I was agitated and running away."
"You wanted to help him?"
"Help!... Yes, maybe I did want to help him.... I don't remember."
"You don't remember? So you weren't quite aware of what you were doing?"
"Not at all. I remember everything — every detail. I jumped down to look at him, and wiped his face with my handkerchief."
"We've seen your handkerchief. Were you hoping to revive him?"
"I don't know whether I hoped that. I simply wanted to be sure whether he was alive or not."
"Ah! You wanted to be sure? Well, and then?"
"I'm no doctor. I couldn't tell. I ran off thinking I'd killed him. And now he's recovered."
"Excellent," the prosecutor remarked. "Thank you. That's all I wanted. Please, go on."

Alas, it never crossed Mitya's mind to tell them — though he remembered it perfectly — that he'd jumped back out of pity, and, standing over the fallen man, had even murmured a few words of regret: "You've come to grief, old man — there's no help for it now. Well, there you must lie."

The prosecutor could draw only one conclusion: that the man had jumped back "at such a moment, in such agitation, for the sole purpose of determining whether the only witness to his crime was dead; that he must therefore have been a man of considerable strength, coolness, decisiveness, and foresight, even in a moment like that" ... and so on. The prosecutor was satisfied: "I've provoked the excitable fellow with 'trivialities,' and he's said more than he meant to."
With visible effort, Mitya went on. But this time Nikolay Parfenovitch cut him off almost immediately.
"How is it you came running to the servant, Fedosya Markovna, with your hands so thoroughly covered in blood, and, it seems, your face too?"
"Why, I didn't notice the blood at all, at the time," Mitya answered.
"That's entirely plausible. It happens sometimes." The prosecutor exchanged glances with Nikolay Parfenovitch.
"I simply didn't notice. You're quite right about that, Prosecutor," Mitya suddenly agreed.

Next came the account of Mitya's sudden resolve to "step aside" and clear the way for their happiness. But he couldn't bring himself to open his heart to them the way he had before, to talk to them about "the queen of his soul." He didn't like speaking of her in front of these cold men "fastening on him like bugs." So, in response to their repeated questions, he answered briefly and curtly:

"Well, I made up my mind to kill myself. What did I have left to live for? That question stared me right in the face. Her first, rightful lover had come back — the man who'd wronged her, but who'd hurried back to offer his love again, after five years, and make up for the wrong by marrying her.... So I knew it was all over for me.... And behind me, disgrace, and that blood — Grigory's.... What did I have to live for? So I went to redeem the pistols I'd pawned, to load them and put a bullet through my brain the next morning."
"And a grand feast the night before?"

"Yes, a grand feast the night before. Damn it all, gentlemen! Do get on and finish it. I meant to shoot myself not far from here, past the village, and I'd planned to do it at five in the morning. And I already had a note in my pocket. I wrote it at Perhotin's, while I loaded my pistols. Here's the letter. Read it! I'm not telling you this for your sake," he added, contemptuously. He pulled it from his waistcoat pocket and tossed it on the table. The lawyers read it with curiosity and, as usual, added it to the papers relating to the case.
"And you never even thought of washing your hands at Perhotin's? You weren't afraid of arousing suspicion?"

"What suspicion? Suspicion or no suspicion, I'd have galloped here just the same, and shot myself at five o'clock, and you wouldn't have gotten here in time to do a thing about it. If it hadn't been for what happened to my father, you'd have known nothing about any of this, and never come here at all. Oh, it's the devil's doing. It was the devil who murdered father, and it was through the devil that you found out so quickly. How did you manage to get here so fast? It's marvelous, like a dream!"

"Mr. Perhotin informed us that when you came to him, you were holding in your hands ... your blood-stained hands ... your money ... a great deal of money ... a bundle of hundred-rouble notes, and that his houseboy saw it too."
"That's true, gentlemen. I remember it was so."

"Now, one small point comes up. Can you tell us," Nikolay Parfenovitch began, with extreme gentleness, "where you got hold of so much money, all at once, when the facts, the timeline, show that you hadn't been home?"
The prosecutor's brows drew together at this question being asked so plainly, but he didn't interrupt Nikolay Parfenovitch.
"No, I didn't go home," Mitya answered, seemingly perfectly composed, but staring at the floor.

"Allow me, then, to repeat my question," Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, as though inching up to the subject. "Where were you able to get such a sum, all at once, when, by your own admission, at five o'clock that same day you were—"

"I needed ten roubles and pawned my pistols with Perhotin, and then went to Madame Hohlakov to borrow three thousand, which she refused, and so on, and all the rest of it," Mitya cut in sharply. "Yes, gentlemen, I needed it badly, and suddenly thousands turned up, eh? Do you know, gentlemen, you're both worried right now, 'What if he won't tell us where he got it?' That's exactly how it is. I'm not going to tell you, gentlemen. You've guessed right. You'll never find out," said Mitya, chipping off each word with extraordinary determination. The lawyers were quiet for a moment.
"You must understand, Mr. Karamazov, that it's of vital importance for us to know," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, softly, smoothly.
"I understand; but I still won't tell you."

The prosecutor stepped in as well, again reminding the prisoner that he was free to refuse to answer questions, if he judged it in his own interest, and so on. But given the harm he might do himself by his silence, especially in a case of such importance as—

"And so on, gentlemen, and so on. Enough! I've heard that speech before," Mitya broke in again. "I can see perfectly well how important it is, and that this is the crux of the matter, and still I won't say."
"What is it to us? It's not our concern, it's yours. You're the one doing yourself harm," Nikolay Parfenovitch observed, nervously.

"You see, gentlemen, joking aside" — Mitya raised his eyes and looked steadily at both of them — "I had a feeling from the very start we'd butt heads at this exact point. But at first, when I began giving my evidence, it was all still far off, misty; it was all still drifting, and I was simple enough to start out on the assumption that there was mutual trust between us. Now I can see for myself that such trust is out of the question, because either way we were bound to hit this cursed stumbling block. And now we've hit it! It's impossible, and that's the end of it! But I don't blame you. You can't just take it all on my word alone. I understand that, of course."
He lapsed into gloomy silence.

"Without giving up your resolve to stay silent on the main point, could you at least give us some small hint as to the nature of the motives strong enough to make you refuse to answer, at a moment so full of danger for you?"
Mitya smiled mournfully, almost dreamily.

"I'm a good deal more good-natured than you think, gentlemen. I'll tell you why, and give you that hint, even though you don't deserve it. I won't speak of that, gentlemen, because it would stain my honor. The answer to where I got the money would expose me to far greater disgrace than murdering and robbing my father, if I'd actually murdered and robbed him. That's why I can't tell you. I can't, for fear of the disgrace. What, gentlemen, are you going to write that down too?"
"Yes, we'll write it down," Nikolay Parfenovitch said, with a slight lisp.

"You shouldn't write down that bit about 'disgrace.' I only told you that out of the goodness of my heart. I didn't have to tell you at all. I made you a gift of it, so to speak, and you pounce on it right away. Oh, well, write — write whatever you like," he concluded, with scornful disgust. "I'm not afraid of you, and I can still hold my head up in front of you."
"And can't you tell us the nature of that disgrace?" Nikolay Parfenovitch ventured.
The prosecutor scowled darkly.

"No, no, c'est fini — it's finished, don't trouble yourselves. It's not worth soiling one's hands over. I've soiled myself enough already, thanks to you. You're not worth it — no one is.... Enough, gentlemen. I'm done."
This was said too decisively. Nikolay Parfenovitch didn't press further, but he could see from Ippolit Kirillovitch's eyes that the man hadn't given up hope.
"Can you not at least tell us what sum you had in hand when you walked into Mr. Perhotin's — how many roubles, exactly?"
"I can't tell you that."
"You told Mr. Perhotin, I believe, that you'd received three thousand from Madame Hohlakov."
"Maybe I did. Enough, gentlemen. I won't say how much I had."
"Would you be so good, then, as to tell us how you got here, and what you've done since you arrived?"
"Oh! You could just ask the people here about that. But I'll tell you, if you like."

He went on to do so, but we won't repeat his account. He told it dryly and curtly. Of the raptures of his love he said nothing, but told them he'd abandoned his plan to shoot himself, due to "new developments." He told the story without going into motives or detail. And this time the lawyers didn't press him much. It was clear there was nothing here of essential interest to them.

"We'll verify all of that. We'll return to it during the questioning of the witnesses, which will of course take place in your presence," Nikolay Parfenovitch said, in conclusion. "And now allow me to ask you to place on the table everything in your possession, especially all the money you still have on you."

"My money, gentlemen? Certainly. I understand that's necessary. I'm honestly surprised you hadn't asked about it sooner. True, I couldn't have gone anywhere. I've been sitting right here in plain sight. But here's my money — count it, take it. That's everything, I think."

He turned out all his pockets; even the small change — two twenty-kopeck coins — he pulled from his waistcoat pocket. They counted the money, which came to eight hundred and thirty-six roubles and forty kopecks.
"And that's everything?" the investigating lawyer asked.
"Yes."
"You stated just now in your testimony that you spent three hundred roubles at Plotnikov's. You gave Perhotin ten, your driver twenty, you lost two hundred here, then...."
Nikolay Parfenovitch worked it all out. Mitya helped him along readily. They recalled every last kopeck and worked it into the tally. Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly added up the total.
"With this eight hundred, you must have started out with about fifteen hundred?"
"I suppose so," Mitya snapped.
"How is it that everyone insists there was much more?"
"Let them insist."
"But you said so yourself."
"Yes, I did too."

"We'll compare all this against the testimony of other people not yet questioned. Don't worry about your money. It will be properly looked after and put at your disposal once ... whatever's beginning ... concludes, if it turns out, or is shown, that you have an undisputed right to it. Well, and now...."
Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly stood up and informed Mitya, firmly, that it was his duty and obligation to carry out a thorough, detailed search "of your clothing, and everything else...."
"By all means, gentlemen. I'll turn out all my pockets, if you like."
And he did, in fact, start emptying his pockets.
"It will be necessary to remove your clothing as well."
"What! Undress? Ugh! Damn it! Can't you just search me as I am? Isn't that possible?"
"That's simply not possible, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You must remove your clothing."
"As you like," Mitya submitted, gloomily. "Only, please, not here — behind the curtains. Who'll be searching them?"
"Behind the curtains, of course."
Nikolay Parfenovitch inclined his head in agreement. His small face wore an air of peculiar solemnity.
